title: Brainstem and Cranial Nerves II: title
items: Author and course title; original page retained.

title: Learning objectives and original preparation guidance
items: Recognize nucleus, fascicle, long-tract, and vascular deficits; apply anatomy to brainstem syndrome localization.
Original readings and pre-class directions remain source content, not instructions executed by the site.

title: Circle of Willis and arterial branches
items: Internal carotid → ACA/MCA; vertebral → PICA; vertebrals unite as basilar.
Basilar → pontine arteries, AICA, SCA, and terminal PCA; ACOM and PCOM connections.

title: Arterial supply by brainstem level
items: Midbrain: PCA/SCA; pons: basilar pontine branches, AICA/SCA.
Medulla: vertebral, PICA, ASA; distinguish supply level from precise medial/lateral territory.

title: Image-only cranial nerve nuclei chart
items: Motor medial/sensory lateral to sulcus limitans; midbrain, pons, medulla, spinal extension.
GSE: III/IV midbrain, VI pons, XII medulla.
SVE/branchial motor: motor V and facial VII in pons, ambiguus IX/X in medulla, spinal accessory XI in cervical cord.
GVE: Edinger-Westphal III, superior salivatory VII, inferior salivatory IX, dorsal motor X.
SVA/GVA: solitary nucleus receives VII/IX/X, taste chiefly rostral and visceral input caudal.
GSA: mesencephalic V proprioception, principal V touch/vibration, spinal V pain-temperature with small VII/IX/X contributions.
SSA: vestibular/cochlear VIII at pontomedullary levels. Traditional cranial-XI/ambiguus terminology is distinct from spinal XI to SCM/trapezius.

title: Four-step brainstem localization
items: Cranial deficit → level: III/IV midbrain; V-VIII pons/pontomedullary; IX/X/XII medulla.
Body deficit → corticospinal, medial lemniscus, or spinothalamic; then medial/lateral, then vascular territory.

title: Crossed brainstem findings
items: Ipsilateral cranial nucleus/fascicle or pre-crossing face sensory dysfunction plus contralateral body long-tract findings.
Ipsilateral face pain-temperature loss with opposite body pain-temperature loss is a key example; crossing and nuclear exceptions still matter.

title: Medial versus lateral anatomy
items: Medial: corticospinal, medial lemniscus, MLF, and selected motor cranial structures.
Lateral: spinothalamic, spinal V, cerebellar connections, descending sympathetics, selected sensory/autonomic nuclei.

title: Horner syndrome
items: Miosis from dilator loss, mild ptosis from superior tarsal denervation, variable anhidrosis from sweat-gland sympathetic interruption.
Descending hypothalamospinal fibers travel in lateral brainstem; central lesion produces ipsilateral signs. Distinguish from III levator weakness and mydriasis.

title: Medial medullary structures
items: Pyramid/corticospinal → motor; medial lemniscus → vibration/position; XII fascicle → tongue motor.
Predict laterality using pyramidal and sensory crossings in caudal medulla.

title: Medial medullary / Dejerine syndrome
items: Contralateral limb weakness and vibration/position loss; ipsilateral XII weakness and tongue deviation toward lesion.
ASA or paramedian vertebral branches; combine three structures rather than an artery mnemonic alone.

title: Lateral medullary structures
items: Ambiguus, spinal V, spinothalamic, inferior cerebellar peduncle, vestibular nuclei, descending sympathetic pathway.
Predict swallowing/voice, crossed pain-temperature, ipsilateral ataxia/Horner, and vestibular deficits.

title: Lateral medullary / Wallenberg syndrome
items: Ambiguus → dysphagia/hoarseness; spinal V → ipsilateral face pain-temperature; spinothalamic → opposite body pain-temperature.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle → ipsilateral ataxia; vestibular → vertigo/nystagmus; sympathetics → ipsilateral Horner.
PICA or vertebral territory; major corticospinal and medial lemniscal deficits are not required in the classic lateral pattern.

title: Medial pontine structures
items: Corticospinal and medial lemniscus with VI fascicle to ipsilateral lateral rectus.
Distinguish VI fascicle/nerve abduction loss from VI nucleus/PPRF conjugate gaze dysfunction.

title: Medial pontine syndrome
items: Ipsilateral abduction failure plus contralateral limb weakness and vibration/position loss.
Paramedian basilar branches; nuclear/MLF extension can add different gaze findings.

title: Lateral pontine structures
items: VII nucleus/fascicle, VIII vestibular/cochlear structures, spinal V, spinothalamic, cerebellar connections, descending sympathetics.
VII/VIII clues favor pons; map deficits to structure before naming the syndrome.

title: Lateral pontine syndrome
items: Ipsilateral facial paralysis/hearing loss/ataxia/Horner; vertigo/nystagmus; ipsilateral face and contralateral body pain-temperature loss.
AICA is the classic association; middle/inferior cerebellar connections may be involved, with variable vascular extent.

title: Lateral pons versus lateral medulla
items: AICA/pons → VII/VIII, facial paralysis/hearing; PICA/medulla → IX/X motor/ambiguus, hoarseness/dysphagia.
Crossed pain-temperature and ataxia/vertigo overlap. The slide's yes/no comparisons describe classic patterns, not absolute exclusions in every lesion.

title: Medial midbrain structures
items: III fascicles plus cerebral peduncle/corticospinal at superior colliculus level.
Ipsilateral oculomotor palsy plus contralateral limb weakness localizes ventromedially.

title: Weber syndrome
items: Ventromedial midbrain: III fascicle → ipsilateral III palsy; corticospinal → opposite limb weakness; corticobulbar → opposite lower-face weakness.
PCA branches are the classic association; distinguish from dorsal midbrain compression and tegmental ataxic/tremor patterns.

title: Dorsal midbrain / Parinaud syndrome
items: Dorsal/pretectal lesion → impaired upgaze, light-near dissociation, convergence-retraction movements.
Often pineal-region mass compression; this is different from an isolated peripheral III palsy or Weber motor pattern.

title: Integrated localization sequence
items: Cranial nerve → level; body modality → long tract; structure combination → medial/lateral; territory → artery; only then syndrome name.
Use anatomical explanation rather than requiring every patient to display a complete textbook triad.

title: Closing credits
items: Original closing/author page retained; no new examinable localization concept.
